issues.title: Septic shock in theatre, dialysis choices and more brands bowing out
tldr: In 584 patients with septic shock having source-control surgery, adding dobutamine (5 µg/kg/min) to noradrenaline during the operation cut postoperative AKI from 34.7% to 22.8% (JAMA). It's a surrogate outcome with more tachycardia, so it's worth a look but isn't settled.

A big JAMA/NEJM week for ICU: ICRAKI found starting with intermittent haemodialysis wasn't non-inferior to CRRT and 90-day mortality was higher (63.1% vs 53.5%). SAVE-ICU's isoflurane sedation and VASSPR's earlier vasopressin threshold both made no difference to mortality.

Supply: Juno sugammadex is being discontinued (deletion 31 Dec), and Hypnovel 5 mg/5 mL midazolam (30 Oct) and Juno noradrenaline 2 mg/2 mL (30 Nov) are leaving the market. Other brands are available, but expect trolley changes. This issue covers two weeks, as there was no issue on 12 Oct.

items.title: Septic shock in theatre: adding dobutamine to noradrenaline reduced postoperative AKI
items.design: Open-label multicentre RCT · 39 hospitals in China · n=584
items.finding: Adults with septic shock having surgical source control were randomised to intraoperative dobutamine 5 µg/kg/min (halved if heart rate exceeded 130/min or arrhythmia developed) plus noradrenaline, or noradrenaline alone. New or worsening AKI within 7 days fell from 34.7% to 22.8% (adjusted RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.49–0.83). Day-28 mortality (16.2% vs 20.4%) and need for kidney replacement therapy didn't differ significantly, and tachycardia above 100/min was more common with dobutamine (41.0% vs 29.9%).
items.trust: Moderate. It's a sizeable multicentre trial, but open-label, confined to Chinese tertiary centres, and the primary outcome is a surrogate. The control AKI rate was lower than the trial assumed when planning.
items.soWhat: For the septic laparotomy at 2 am, low-dose dobutamine alongside noradrenaline is a plausible way to protect the kidneys. One trial with no hard-outcome benefit isn't enough to make it routine; watch the heart rate.

items.title: ICRAKI: starting with intermittent haemodialysis wasn't non-inferior to CRRT
items.design: Open-label non-inferiority RCT · 42 French ICUs · n=554 (535 analysed) · stopped early
items.finding: Critically ill adults with AKI needing renal replacement started on either intermittent haemodialysis or continuous RRT. The primary outcome (death, dialysis dependence or persisting kidney dysfunction at 90 days) occurred in 78.1% vs 71.6% (adjusted difference 6.28 points, 95% CI −1.22 to 13.79), so IHD failed the 7.5-point non-inferiority margin. Day-90 mortality, a secondary outcome, was 63.1% vs 53.5% (HR 1.30, 1.04–1.63).
items.trust: Moderate. Stopping early, at about half the planned 1,000 patients, can exaggerate effects. The trial was open-label, and the delivered IHD dose was below target. The mortality finding is secondary.
items.soWhat: Mainly for intensivists: it supports CRRT as the default first modality in ICU AKI. Worth knowing if you work in ICU or are handing over an unstable post-op patient who will need dialysis.

items.title: SAVE-ICU: isoflurane sedation in hypoxaemic respiratory failure didn't save lives
items.design: Pragmatic open-label RCT · 14 Canadian ICUs · n=780 analysed
items.finding: Ventilated adults with acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure had isoflurane-based inhaled sedation or usual IV sedation. Hospital mortality was 42.5% vs 43.8% (RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.84–1.14), and ventilator-free days were similar. The inhaled group had fewer delirium- and coma-free days and needed more rescue therapy for hypoxaemia (63.9% vs 55.0%).
items.trust: Moderate to high for the main question. It's a decent-sized multicentre trial, but open-label, with heavy IV co-sedation in the inhaled arm and some patients who never received isoflurane.
items.soWhat: This fits the expert review in our last issue: volatile sedation in the ICU hasn't earned routine use. It doesn't speak to volatiles in theatre.

items.title: VASSPR: starting vasopressin earlier in septic shock didn't change mortality
items.design: Pragmatic cluster-crossover strategy trial · 13 US hospitals · n=3,959
items.finding: Hospitals were randomised month by month, crossing over between starting vasopressin 0.03 U/min at a noradrenaline-equivalent dose of 0.1 µg/kg/min and starting it at 0.4 µg/kg/min. 28-day mortality was 31.8% vs 33.0%, with no significant difference (P=.62). New or persisting cardiogenic shock was 7.4% with the lower threshold vs 6.3%.
items.trust: Moderate. It's large and pragmatic, but the separation between strategies was modest and adherence to the lower threshold was under half, so a real effect could be diluted.
items.soWhat: No reason to change when you add vasopressin. A noradrenaline-sparing second agent remains a judgement call, not a mortality intervention.

items.title: Acute normovolaemic haemodilution in women having cardiac surgery: more hypotension, no fewer transfusions
items.design: Post hoc secondary analysis of the ANH RCT · 32 centres, 11 countries · 405 women
items.finding: Among women in the ANH trial (at least 650 mL whole blood withdrawn before bypass and returned after), allogeneic red cell transfusion was 38.8% with ANH vs 44.6% with usual care (RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.69–1.10). Intraoperative hypotension was more common with ANH (16.0% vs 4.8%; RR 3.30, 1.62–6.74), and ICU stay was about 21 hours longer.
items.trust: Low to moderate. It's an exploratory subgroup that the trial wasn't powered for, so it generates hypotheses rather than answering the question.
items.soWhat: If your unit uses ANH, be ready for intraoperative hypotension in women. Don't count on the transfusion benefit seen in the whole trial holding in this group until it's tested properly.

items.title: Continuous glucose monitors in theatre and ICU: reasonable accuracy, worse when perfusion is poor
items.design: Prospective observational validation study · Copenhagen · n=58
items.finding: Dexcom G7 readings were compared with point-of-care glucose in people with diabetes having surgery or in ICU. Median absolute relative difference was 10.9%, and 98% of 1,212 paired readings fell in the clinically acceptable Clarke zones A and B. Accuracy was worse during hypoperfusion (MARD 4.5 points higher, 95% CI 2.3–6.7), and limits of agreement were wide (−5.6 to 3.4 mM).
items.trust: Low to moderate. A small study of one device, and there was no hypoglycaemia, so accuracy in the range that matters most is untested.
items.soWhat: More patients will turn up wearing a CGM. It's fine for trends in a stable patient, but check a capillary or arterial glucose before acting, especially on vasopressors or if you suspect a low.

items.title: PRoFLUID: most fluid in ventilated ICU patients isn't resuscitation
items.design: International prospective cohort · 206 ICUs in 41 countries · n=2,454
items.finding: Median fluid input was 3.0 L on day 1, falling to 2.6 L by day 6. Over the first three days, maintenance or replacement (31.9%) and fluid creep from drugs and flushes (30.9%) far outweighed resuscitation alone (16.0%). Balanced crystalloids made up 48.9% of fluid and 0.9% saline 27.0%, with large variation between ICUs.
items.trust: Good for describing practice; it's observational and doesn't link fluid volumes to outcomes.
items.soWhat: Fluid creep from drug carriers and line flushes is a big share of the total, in theatre as well as ICU. It's worth counting when you're trying to run a patient dry.

items.title: Sugammadex: Juno brand being discontinued, Viatris still limited
items.dateNote: Status as checked on 19 Oct; the date the Juno listing first appeared isn't shown
items.finding: Sugammadex Juno 200 mg/2 mL is listed as 'to be discontinued', with deletion from the market on 31 Dec 2026 and reduced supply until stock runs out. Viatris 200 mg/2 mL remains limited until 23 Oct, Accord is unavailable until 31 Mar 2027, and Lupin is still due for deletion on 31 Jan 2027. Medsurge 500 mg/5 mL was resolved on 5 Oct.
items.soWhat: That's another brand leaving a crowded field. Expect more brand switches, and check with theatre pharmacy which presentations you'll be stocking in the new year.

items.title: Brand exits: Hypnovel midazolam, Juno noradrenaline and Precedex vials
items.dateNote: Status as checked on 19 Oct; the dates the listings first appeared aren't shown
items.finding: Three familiar presentations are listed as 'to be discontinued', each with alternative brands available: Hypnovel midazolam 5 mg/5 mL ampoules (deletion 30 Oct 2026), Noradrenaline Juno 2 mg/2 mL ampoules (deletion 30 Nov 2026, reduced supply until exhausted) and Precedex dexmedetomidine 200 µg/2 mL vials (deletion 1 Feb 2027).
items.soWhat: None is a shortage of the drug itself, but the packaging on the trolley may change. Worth flagging to anaesthetic nurses and checking that infusion protocols name the drug and concentration, not a brand.

items.title: Also listed: dexamethasone, magnesium and buprenorphine injection
items.finding: Dexamethasone Juno 4 mg/1 mL has been limited since 15 Oct, with supply expected 20 Nov. Medsurge magnesium sulfate 50% 2.5 g/5 mL has been limited since 13 Oct, until 13 Dec. The long-running Temgesic buprenorphine 300 µg/1 mL shortage (since 2021) was updated on 12 Oct and now runs to 31 Mar 2027. It's the only buprenorphine injection listed, and the TGA advises considering alternative treatments. DBL dexamethasone 8 mg/2 mL is due for deletion on 1 Oct 2027.
items.soWhat: Dexamethasone and magnesium are brand substitutions; check what the obstetric unit is stocking. There's no alternative brand for injectable buprenorphine, so plan other options for patients who rely on it.

items.title: National Anaesthesia Day: ANZCA's fasting message focuses on GLP-1s and peptides
items.dateNote: Media release 5 Oct, ahead of National Anaesthesia Day on 16 Oct
items.finding: ANZCA's 2026 National Anaesthesia Day campaign warned patients that GLP-1 drugs and unapproved peptides can affect fasting, citing the UK cohort in our last issue. Its patient fact sheet keeps the 6-hour limit for food and allows adults clear fluids (up to 200 mL an hour) until called to theatre. It says people on GLP-1 drugs must tell their anaesthetist and may be asked to have only clear fluids for 24 hours beforehand, and it names retatrutide and other peptides. Patients are told not to stop their medication on their own.
items.soWhat: Your patients may arrive having read this. Make sure your preadmission instructions match it, and ask specifically about peptides and online supplies as well as prescribed GLP-1s.

items.title: ASA's inquiry submission forecasts a shortfall of hundreds of anaesthetists by 2032
items.finding: In its submission to the House of Representatives inquiry into specialist access and affordability, the ASA projects demand for anaesthesia growing faster than the workforce (35.7% vs 31.8%, 2017–2032), leaving a shortfall of 343 anaesthetists in 2032, or 507 if individual workloads fall. It calls for at least 50 extra trainee posts a year, a third of them regional or rural, and an independent review of MBS anaesthesia benefits, noting the RVG unit value rose 34.7% from 2001 to 2025 against CPI growth of 91.6%.
items.soWhat: Useful numbers for any conversation about fees and gap payments. The separate government consultation on 'excessive' specialist fees closes today (19 Oct).

quickHits.text: ANESTHESIOLOGY 2026 abstract (press release only): noise-cancelling headphones during minimally invasive gynaecological surgery cut 48-hour PONV from 52.1% to 35.4% in an RCT of 192 women.

ANESTHESIOLOGY 2026 abstract: in a meta-analysis of 6 RCTs (n=1,832), ketamine or esketamine at caesarean modestly lowered early postnatal depression scores (SMD −0.36). The authors say it's too early to claim prevention.

ANESTHESIOLOGY 2026 abstract: at one US centre, patients who smoked or vaped cannabis needed more initial propofol for upper endoscopy (about 193 mg vs 151 mg in non-users). Edible users didn't, but the groups were small.

Robot-assisted radical hysterectomy had fewer intraoperative complications than open surgery (5.7% vs 10.0%) but similar 30-day complications (about a third in each arm) in a secondary analysis of the 900-patient RACC trial.

US FDA (5 Oct): BD is removing some Alaris pump infusion sets used with the model 8100 pump module. At rates below 1 mL/h and boluses of 5 mL or less they can under- or over-infuse or delay occlusion alarms, with neonatal, paediatric and critical-care patients most at risk. It's a US action, so check whether your hospital uses the affected sets.

issues.coverage: This issue covers two weeks (6–19 Oct), as there was no issue on 12 Oct. Indexing services (Crossref, Europe PMC, PubMed) and most anaesthesia publisher sites (BJA, Wiley, LWW, Sage) couldn't be read, so many in-window anaesthesia papers were seen as titles only and left out rather than guessed at. These include a European study of general anaesthesia rates in 9,989 caesarean deliveries (BJA), pain scores and intrapartum fever with epidurals (BJA), socioeconomic position in PQIP (BJA), a ketamine/esketamine delirium meta-analysis and a consensus statement on anaesthesia for advanced bronchoscopy (both A&A). Anesthesiology, Anaesthesia, AIC, NEJM (apart from ICRAKI), Lancet, BMJ, Annals of Surgery and BJS were largely unchecked. ICRAKI's numbers come from trial summaries rather than the NEJM page. ANESTHESIOLOGY 2026 items are meeting abstracts reported in press releases, not peer-reviewed papers. Several TGA shortage pages (neostigmine, suxamethonium, metaraminol, ropivacaine, lidocaine, heparin) returned errors, and no new ANZCA safety alert was visible in the window, so check the live database.

issues.title: Blood choices, GLP-1 stomachs and a quiet research week
tldr: Jehovah's Witnesses now leave decisions on donor red cells, plasma, platelets and white cells to individual conscience (whole blood is still refused). Don't assume either way: ask each patient specifically and document it.

In a UK national cohort of 47,039 patients, regurgitation or aspiration was about 11 times more common in GLP-1 RA users (1 in 71 vs 1 in 802), and over 40% got the drug outside usual prescribing. Ask about online supplies.

Supply: Lupin's sugammadex is being discontinued (deletion 31 Jan 2027), Viatris 200 mg/2 mL stays limited to 23 Oct, and B. Braun propofol 1% 100 mL is still out until mid-January. A thin week for new papers, see the coverage note.

items.title: GLP-1 RAs and the stomach: a UK national cohort puts a number on regurgitation
items.dateNote: Published mid-September (16–17 Sep) alongside the Association of Anaesthetists annual meeting in Liverpool; catch-up, as it missed the last issue
items.design: Prospective national multicentre cohort · 119 UK sites · n=47,039
items.finding: Across adults having elective or emergency procedures with anaesthetic care, 1,348 patients (2.9%, about 1 in 36) were taking a GLP-1 receptor agonist. Regurgitation or pulmonary aspiration occurred in about 1 in 71 GLP-1 RA users versus 1 in 802 non-users, roughly an 11-fold difference. More than 40% of users obtained the drug outside GP or hospital prescribing, for example from online pharmacies.
items.trust: Moderate. It's large, prospective and national, but observational: users differ from non-users, and the 11-fold figure is the headline ratio from the press release. We couldn't open the full paper to check adjusted estimates or event counts.
items.soWhat: Ask every patient directly about GLP-1 RAs, including online or compounded supplies, because the medication list won't always show them. Follow your local GLP-1 RA pathway, and keep regurgitation in mind at induction and emergence.

items.title: Robotic hip and knee replacement: no better than conventional at 2.5 years
items.design: Twin target-trial emulations (separate hip and knee papers) · UK National Joint Registry 2018–24 · hips n=666,283 (10,203 robotic), knees n=697,145 (22,111 robotic)
items.finding: After propensity-score matching, robotic-assisted surgery showed no difference from conventional surgery in implant survival, overall revision or intraoperative complications over a mean 2.5 years. Robotic hips had fewer revisions for implant malpositioning, but no fewer revisions overall. The authors put the extra cost at about £1m upfront plus £1,000–2,500 per patient.
items.trust: Moderate. Very large, but observational, with possible unmeasured confounding (surgeon experience, case selection) and short follow-up. Functional outcomes weren't measured; RCTs such as RACER are still running.
items.soWhat: Nothing changes for the anaesthetic, but expect robotic arthroplasty to come up when theatre time and budgets are planned. So far the extra cost isn't buying lower overall revision rates.

items.title: Jehovah's Witnesses: blood components now a matter of individual conscience
items.dateNote: Policy announced 18 Sep; APSF practice update 24 Sep
items.finding: The Governing Body of Jehovah's Witnesses announced on 18 Sep that accepting donor red cells, white cells, plasma or platelets is now a personal decision. The position against whole blood is unchanged. This follows a March 2026 change allowing autologous collection, storage and transfusion. The APSF says not to assume any patient now accepts blood products, to discuss preferences directly and specifically before an anaesthetic where major bleeding is possible, to document them clearly, and to reconfirm previously documented choices.
items.soWhat: Advance directives and consent forms written before September may no longer reflect what a patient would accept. Revisit them for elective cardiac, obstetric and major surgery, and flag the change to your blood management and obstetric teams. We found no ANZCA or Lifeblood statement yet.

items.title: Sugammadex: Lupin brand to be discontinued; propofol 100 mL still short
items.dateNote: As listed when we checked on 4–5 Oct; the TGA pages loaded inconsistently, so check live
items.finding: Sugammadex LAPL (Lupin) is listed as to be discontinued, with supply reducing until exhausted and market deletion on 31 Jan 2027. Viatris 200 mg/2 mL remains limited until 23 Oct, Accord remains unavailable until 31 Mar 2027, and Medsurge 500 mg/5 mL was still listed as limited even though its expected end date of 30 Sep has passed. The TGA notes alternative brands are available. B. Braun Propofol-Lipuro 1% 100 mL remains unavailable until 15 Jan 2027.
items.soWhat: Expect more sugammadex brand changes into next year. Ask pharmacy which brand you'll be stocking after January, and keep neostigmine-based reversal and quantitative monitoring familiar to trainees.

items.title: Neonatal resuscitation hoses: Dräger VentStar Resus Neo recall is Class I in the US
items.dateNote: FDA early alert 3 Sep; classified Class I on 2 Oct
items.finding: Users found cracks in the hose of VentStar Resus Neo breathing circuits (model MP00310) before use. A cracked hose may leak or come off, restricting ventilation or delaying therapy, with a risk of desaturation, hypoxia or death. Dräger advises inspecting hoses before use and discarding any with cracks or a detached hose. No serious injuries or deaths had been reported as of 3 Sep.
items.soWhat: This is a US recall and we couldn't confirm whether these circuits are supplied in Australia. If your birth suite or neonatal resuscitaires use Dräger circuits, check the model and add a hose check to the setup routine.

items.title: Inhaled sedation in ARDS: experts say keep it inside trials for now
items.finding: An international narrative review on volatile sedation for ARDS weighs the physiological rationale against the trial evidence, including SESAR, where sevoflurane gave fewer ventilator-free days and higher mortality than propofol. The authors conclude that routine clinical use of volatile ICU sedation in ARDS isn't currently recommended outside clinical trials.
items.soWhat: If your ICU has, or is considering, an anaesthetic conserving device, reserve it for trials or specific indications rather than routine ARDS sedation.

quickHits.text: PRESSURE (17 UK paediatric ICUs) compared a permissive target, mean arterial pressure at the 5th centile for age, with usual care in ventilated children on vasoactive drugs. It came out in JAMA on 28 Sep, but we couldn't open the results this week. Worth reading if you do paediatric or PICU work.

The Million Anesthesia Cases paediatric fasting analysis is now a full BJA paper (e-pub 28 Sep). In the ANESTHESIOLOGY 2025 abstract (71,835 children, 12 US hospitals), the median clear-fluid fast in 2024 was 8.7 hours, and infants' fasts weren't improving.

In two Philadelphia hospitals, dexmedetomidine use in admissions with opioid use disorder rose from about 6% to about 20% (about 32% in the final quarter) after medetomidine appeared in the fentanyl supply. In that last quarter, a third of patients needed ICU-level care. It's an early warning of a severe withdrawal syndrome.

A multicentre interrupted time-series study looked at shutting off piped nitrous oxide alongside decision support to cut anaesthetic emissions. It's useful background if your hospital is decommissioning its N2O manifold, though we couldn't open the results.
Stem cell-derived human brain 'assembloids' reproduced the slow, synchronised waves of propofol anaesthesia without a thalamus. Lab work, but a neat teaching point on how anaesthesia might work.

issues.coverage: A hard week to read. Most publisher sites (BJA, Wiley, LWW, JAMA Network, NEJM, Lancet, PubMed) blocked automated reading, and search indexes lagged behind the window. So we could confirm several in-window papers but not their results, and left them out rather than guess: J-PEDIA supraglottic airways in children with airway hyperresponsiveness, cannabis and anaesthetic dosing, and a French survey on neuromuscular blockade guideline adherence (all BJA). The PRESSURE results and the GLP-1 cohort's adjusted estimates also couldn't be checked. NEJM, Lancet, Annals of Surgery, BJS, CCM, EJA, RAPM, AIC and JCA weren't checked. We found no ANZCA safety alert or TGA recall dated in the window, but the ANZCA and TGA sites didn't fully load. TGA shortage listings were inconsistent between page versions, so check the live database.

issues.title: Infant airways, a propofol squeeze, and the TIVA answer
tldr: Propofol 1% 100 mL (B. Braun) is unavailable until mid-January and several sugammadex brands are short or gone, so check with theatre pharmacy.
In neonates and infants, videolaryngoscopy gave a better view but lower first-attempt success than direct laryngoscopy (Japanese registry, 3,250 intubations).
Catch-up: VITAL (JAMA, August) found TIVA versus volatile made no difference to days at home or survival in 2,508 over-50s having major surgery. Choose on PONV risk and patient factors.

items.title: Videolaryngoscopy in neonates and infants: better view, lower first-pass success
items.finding: Compared with direct laryngoscopy, using a videolaryngoscope for the first attempt gave a better glottic view (+17.8 percentage points). But first-attempt success was lower (adjusted RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.83–0.96) and desaturation was about twice as common (adjusted RR 2.18).
items.trust: Moderate. It's observational, and VL was probably chosen for harder airways despite the propensity weighting.
items.soWhat: In small infants a better view on the screen didn't translate into first-attempt success. Train tube delivery and technique rather than assuming VL is automatically the safer first choice.

items.title: Compress the internal jugular while threading a subclavian wire: fewer malpositioned lines
items.design: Single-centre RCT · elective neurosurgical adults · n=315
items.finding: During ultrasound-guided right infraclavicular subclavian cannulation, pressing the probe on the same-side internal jugular vein while advancing the guidewire cut catheter malposition from 13% to 6% (OR 0.42, 95% CI 0.18–0.95). It added about 25 seconds.
items.trust: Moderate. A single centre and a single surgical population, and the confidence interval sits close to no effect.
items.soWhat: A free, low-risk manoeuvre to try on your next subclavian line, and an easy one to teach.

items.title: After a perioperative catastrophe, most anaesthetists feel unfit to carry on
items.design: Survey of US ASA members, repeating a 2012 survey · n=1,725 · 7% response
items.finding: 94% had been involved in at least one catastrophe. After their most memorable one, 69% felt impaired in the first four hours and 62% at 24 hours. About one in five said they never fully recovered emotionally, the same as in 2012. Formal debriefs and time off were uncommon, and nearly a quarter considered leaving the specialty.
items.trust: Low to moderate. A 7% response invites selection bias and recall bias is likely, but the results point the same way as the 2012 survey.
items.soWhat: Relief from the list and a structured debrief should be automatic after a catastrophe, not something people have to ask for. Worth checking what your department's actual process is.

items.title: Which prehab exercise works? Aerobic plus breathing training leads
items.finding: Aerobic, respiratory (pulmonary) and functional training combined ranked best for fewer complications (OR 0.16, very low certainty) and shorter stay (−3.4 days, moderate certainty). Aerobic plus strength training ranked best for quality of life. No programme improved physical recovery.
items.trust: Low. About three-quarters of the trials were at high risk of bias, heterogeneity was large, and a complication effect this big hints at small-study bias.
items.soWhat: If you refer patients to prehab or design a programme, prioritise aerobic work and respiratory training. Don't promise a faster functional recovery.

items.title: NIRS-guided cardiac surgery: a hint of cognitive benefit, nothing harder
items.finding: NIRS-guided management reduced early postoperative cognitive decline (RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.42–0.99, moderate certainty). It did not clearly reduce delirium (RR 0.78, 0.56–1.09), stroke or mortality.
items.trust: Low to moderate. The trials were mostly small and single-centre, with different thresholds and response algorithms, and cognition was measured with brief screens in the first week.
items.soWhat: Not enough to make cerebral oximetry mandatory. If you use it, pair it with a defined response algorithm, as the trials did.

items.title: Malignant hyperthermia risk isn't one-size-fits-all across RYR1 variants
items.design: UK MH Unit data 1988–2025 · 375 index cases and 502 relatives · Bayesian modelling
items.finding: The estimated prevalence of clinical MH susceptibility was about 1 in 38,800. Risk varied up to 125-fold between 28 RYR1 variants. The falling incidence didn't fit simple autosomal dominant inheritance, and the authors favour a threshold model.
items.trust: Moderate. The conclusions depend heavily on the modelling, and UK Biobank under-represents non-White populations.
items.soWhat: Useful when counselling families about a variant result: carrying an RYR1 variant doesn't carry a fixed risk. Trigger-free anaesthesia for susceptible patients doesn't change.

items.title: Intraoperative ketamine didn't reduce long-term opioid use after spine surgery
items.design: Propensity-matched EHR cohort (TriNetX, US) · about 55,700 patients
items.finding: In opioid-naive patients, intraoperative ketamine was linked to slightly more opioid prescribing at 48 hours (RR 1.23) and 6 weeks (RR 1.14), and no difference at 3–12 months. In patients with opioid-use disorder, only the 48-hour difference was seen.
items.trust: Low. There were no dose or timing data, and ketamine was probably given to the harder cases.
items.soWhat: Don't present intraoperative ketamine as protection against persistent opioid use after spine surgery; dose-dependent effects weren't tested. It may still earn its place for acute pain in selected patients.

items.title: TIVA or volatile for major surgery in over-50s: no difference in recovery
items.dateNote: Published online 12 Aug; catch-up in case you missed it
items.design: Pragmatic open-label RCT · 49 UK NHS hospitals · n=2,508
items.finding: Adults aged 50 and over having elective major non-cardiac surgery were randomised to propofol TIVA or volatile maintenance. Days alive and at home at 30 days were almost identical (22.5 vs 22.4; IRR 1.00, 95% CI 0.99–1.02). Mortality to 6 months, major complications (about 12% in each arm) and day-3 QoR-15 did not differ either.
items.trust: High for the main question: large, multicentre and pragmatic. It was open-label, most patients were lower-risk and having abdominal cancer surgery, few were frail, and delirium was checked only once.
items.soWhat: Choose the maintenance technique on patient factors, not on hoped-for outcome gains. PONV favours TIVA (day-1 PONV 27% vs 36%, exploratory). Both awareness cases were in the TIVA arm, a reminder to use processed EEG and to check the line.

items.title: Propofol 1% 100 mL: B. Braun vials unavailable until mid-January
items.finding: B. Braun's Propofol-Lipuro 1% 100 mL is listed as unavailable from 11 Sep 2026 to 15 Jan 2027 because of a jump in demand. Fresenius Kabi's 100 mL vial was also briefly limited (16–23 Sep).
items.soWhat: TIVA and TCI lists that rely on 100 mL vials may feel this. Ask theatre pharmacy which brand and size you're getting.

items.title: Sugammadex: several brands short, others available
items.finding: Viatris 200 mg/2 mL is limited until 23 Oct and Medsurge 500 mg/5 mL until 30 Sep. Accord 200 mg/2 mL has been unavailable since September 2025 and isn't expected back until 31 Mar 2027, and Teva's has been discontinued. The TGA notes other brands remain available.
items.soWhat: Expect brand switches on the drug trolley, and give trainees a heads-up.

items.title: ANZCA updates its alert on a mitochondrial variant and sensitivity to volatile agents
items.dateNote: Alert first issued 4 Jun; updated 17 Sep
items.finding: Fewer than 20 cases over more than 20 years, mostly children and mainly from Venezuela and Chile, of severe neurological deterioration after general anaesthesia have been linked to the mitochondrial DNA variant m.11232T>C, associated with Carabobo state in Venezuela. Volatile agents, particularly sevoflurane, appear to be the main trigger, though ANZCA says the evidence that propofol is safer remains somewhat speculative. The update notes that testing for the variant may now be funded in Australia.
items.soWhat: For patients with maternal Venezuelan ancestry and a suggestive family history, plan a volatile-free anaesthetic (TIVA or regional). Consider whether preadmission screening should ask about this.

items.title: IV line dead space and IV tramadol dosing: ANZCA's September safety update
items.finding: ANZCA updated its alert on drugs left in IV line dead space. In the index case, residual rocuronium from an unflushed line caused re-curarisation in recovery, and small-volume in-line fluid warmers were singled out. The update also reports TGA advice that the recommended maximum daily dose of IV tramadol for acute postoperative pain is 400 mg in otherwise healthy adults.
items.soWhat: Flush lines and remove dead-space devices before transfer, and check that local order sets reflect the 400 mg/day recommended maximum for IV tramadol. The line case would make a good simulation scenario.

items.title: Government consults on 'excessive' specialist fees, with anaesthetists in the spotlight
items.source: Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
items.finding: The consultation sets out six options, from naming fee outliers to caps and penalties. Media coverage singled out anaesthetists as charging furthest above the benchmark among in-hospital specialists. The ASA has argued for system-wide fixes instead of blanket caps: Medicare indexation, transparency on insurer contributions, and informed financial consent.
items.soWhat: Submissions close 19 Oct. It's a good moment to check your informed financial consent process against the ASA's guidance.

items.title: ANZCA 2026.2 Primary written results are out, with vivas in October
items.finding: The list of candidates invited to the Primary viva has been published. The vivas run in October; exact dates and venues weren't on the notice.
items.soWhat: If you supervise or examine, now is the time for viva practice with invited trainees.

items.title: The medical college presidents endorse national pain education standards
items.finding: The Council of Presidents of Medical Colleges has endorsed the Australian Standards for Health Practitioner Pain Management Education, supporting consistent pain teaching across colleges and education providers. The endorsement isn't binding.
items.soWhat: Useful background for anyone designing curricula or teaching sessions; no action needed.

items.title: The UK's redesigned FRCA exam gets GMC approval
items.finding: The new FRCA format launches in July 2027. The first year is a transition period for candidates who have already banked Primary OSCE or SOE results.
items.soWhat: Of interest if you mentor UK-trained registrars or follow exam design; little direct impact in Australia.

quickHits.text: An EMR prompt listing 51 qualifying conditions raised documented ASA ≥3 from 53% to 62% at one US centre (47% to 48% at a control centre). That matters wherever ASA grade drives risk adjustment or RVG modifiers.
Ilofotase alfa didn't reduce AKI after complex cardiac surgery in patients with renal impairment (phase 2 RCT, n=244).
Pooled across the studies with usable data (28 of 50), theatre noise averaged about 71 dB(A), with ENT and orthopaedics the loudest. That's well above WHO guidance for hospital settings.
INSPECT-SR is a new 21-check tool for judging whether an RCT is trustworthy. It's handy for journal club, given anaesthesia's past trial-fabrication scandals.
One in eight women had genito-pelvic pain two months after vaginal birth (French national survey, n=5,802). Low satisfaction with inpatient pain relief was a strong marker.
ObsQoR-10: the suggested minimal important difference is 7–10 points, so smaller gaps between arms probably don't matter to patients.
Basilar artery occlusion at 4.5–24 hours: giving tenecteplase before thrombectomy didn't improve 90-day outcomes (ATTENTION LATE, n=330).
Catch-up: PUMA's new guidelines for providing a foundation for airway management, and for tracheal extubation, came out in Anaesthesia on 26–27 Aug.
